content: Following the completion of data collection and analysis, it is essential to conduct a stakeholder consultation to discuss the results. If the analysis is performed by an organization other than the Ministry of Health, the government may need to validate the preliminary findings before engaging stakeholders. Dissemination of the results can be organized at a national-level roundtable led by the Ministry of Health, where feedback and reflections are solicited from all participants involved in the analysis, including staff and senior management from visited facilities, as well as other partners and donors. This process allows for further triangulation and validation of the findings. The final report should also be disseminated more broadly to the regional and global community, for example, through conferences or other events, to enable other countries and partners to learn from the findings. This dissemination helps prevent duplication of efforts, especially in contexts where multiple partners and NGOs are active in a country or region. The results of the situational analysis should serve as the foundation for developing a national costed roadmap and a set of national targets, which represent the second of eight practical steps. This process can be initiated during the stakeholder consultation to maintain momentum. Individuals and organizations that contributed to the process may also form the core of a national multisectoral coordination mechanism, such as a technical working group or task force, to align and strengthen collaborative efforts. This will drive progress and support the delivery of safe water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) and quality care across the health system. Conducting a situational analysis requires time and resources, and a balance must be struck between the depth of analysis and the available time and budget. Scheduling conflicts and competing priorities may hinder the engagement of some stakeholders, potentially leading to the exclusion of important perspectives. Limited time and budget also constrain the number of facilities that can be visited and assessed. To mitigate these limitations, it is crucial to verify findings and triangulate them with existing assessments and national surveillance data wherever possible. Facility visits should not replace comprehensive survey assessments or surveillance methodologies but should provide a snapshot of conditions and validate information collected from other sources. For example, in Tajikistan (2018), a situational analysis was conducted using a review of the regulatory framework, semi-structured interviews with key actors, and visits to selected healthcare facilities. The findings informed the integration of WASH into the revised National Health Strategy and the National Action Plan to Combat Antimicrobial Resistance. A new standard for WASH in healthcare facilities was developed, and commitments were made by the Ministry of Health and partners to improve WASH services. Similarly, in Serbia (2019), a survey of 320 healthcare facilities was conducted, alongside a qualitative assessment of policies and implementation mechanisms. The results led to stronger collaboration between ministries, the development of practical guidelines, and the integration of WASH into infection prevention and control (IPC) frameworks. A situational analysis provides decision-makers with the evidence needed to take concrete actions to improve WASH in healthcare facilities. The results should guide the development of national targets and a roadmap for achieving universal and sustainable access to quality healthcare, as recommended in the 2019 Resolution on WASH in healthcare facilities. Experiences from various countries demonstrate that such analyses are valuable for fostering collaboration among stakeholders, identifying gaps, and developing comprehensive strategies to improve and sustain WASH in healthcare settings.
